prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of magic-angle flat bands and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is a door opened onto phenomena nobody could previously reach: one tunable material in which flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity can be switched on by a mechanical angle and a gate voltage. The chain is what the prize is meant to reward. Bistritzer and MacDonald made a specific, falsifiable prediction in 2011 (flat bands near a magic angle), and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the original 2018 experiments showing correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. Many independent groups have since reproduced the phases and extended them to other moire systems in under a decade, so the result is experimentally verified and not just attractive. From a microscopy and materials viewpoint it also changed how we think about interfaces, since a twist and a stacking order now serve as design parameters. Three names fit the three-person limit and cover prediction plus original experiment.
statement.case_against: The field is young. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, twist-angle disorder and sample variability remain real concerns, and a prize now could be judged early. The credit is also not clean: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, is outside the credited set, and prior theory on twisted-bilayer band structure and the hBN-encapsulated device work of others are not represented. I take Mehlig's point about this seriously. If the committee cannot be absolutely sure that the people credited did the original work, B024 is the better-documented alternative, with B046 as a second fallback.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B024) are a textbook case of progress limited by measurement precision, with a clean two-person credit to Katori and Ye, 1e-18 performance reproduced by many labs, and a coming redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B024 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I ranked it third myself. Our difference is about what is original. Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock are the invention. Ye's group then brought it to record accuracy, which is excellent but closer to the better, later experiment than the original one. I also still want a clear answer on how far the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems already cover this lineage. I do not think those points sink B024. I would put it first if the committee is not convinced that moire materials are mature enough.

responses.point: Magic-angle graphene (B020) is an elegant theory with a decisive experimental confirmation, but the credit omits Yuan Cao and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and the field is young, so recognition would be early.
responses.response: This is the strongest qualification of my own choice and I accept most of it. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is the explicit magic-angle prediction, and the 2018 experiments realised it, so the prediction-plus-experiment pairing is defensible. But early work on twisted-bilayer band structure is real and the committee must examine it in the record. A prize citation can name the achievement without claiming that nobody else contributed. I disagree with the idea that youth alone is disqualifying. The phases have been reproduced independently in several platforms, which satisfies my verification requirement. I would not wave away the junior-researcher problem, because the three-name limit forces an omission that needs a clear justification.

responses.point: Circuit QED (B042) is the architecture behind essentially all superconducting qubit platforms and very mature, but Girvin's omission is an allocation problem and it follows the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize closely.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your own closeness to this field, and I think the committee should handle that openly. I am not unsympathetic to the physics. Strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon is a real discovery, and the field is mature. My reservations are the one you raise. Four central names must be cut to three, and the proximity to the 2025 prize is a legitimate concern. The committee should not decide the attribution on the basis of who knows the field best. I would keep B042 on the table but not as my first choice this year.

responses.point: IceCube's diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux (B019) is a concrete discovery from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, and the evidence has accumulated for a decade, though a single-person prize is awkward.
responses.response: I agree that this is a genuine new window and I ranked it eighth only because of the attribution. A one-name configuration for a collaboration-scale discovery is the weakness you also note, and I cannot tell from the shortlist who else did the original work. It is also not the same case as a reactor or accelerator experiment, because the instrument is the achievement. Unless someone can supply a defensible set of additional names, I do not think the committee can credit this one safely. I would be glad to be shown the record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can be absolutely sure about the credit for the original 2018 experiments, given Yuan Cao's role and the hBN-device work of other groups.
Whether the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make moire materials too young for a prize this year.
Whether B024 should take priority for its cleaner attribution and its maturity, given the earlier comb and single-quantum-system prizes.
For B046, whether the discovery is the original single-NV detection and control (Wrachtrup and Jelezko) or the later sensing programme including Lukin.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile with any shortlisted candidate or credited person. I note that my colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics and works near superconducting circuits (B042), and that he has said he is close to that field. I have no personal or institutional stake in B042 or its credited names, but I would support his recusal from deciding that ballot's attribution. Several of my long-standing co-authors are in electron microscopy and materials, not in any shortlisted field.
